result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.enumerate_trails()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Enumerate all trails (walks with distinct edges) from source to target. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19802-L19922){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.enumerate_trails( source, target, max_trails=1000, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns the actual sequences of nodes for each trail. A trail is a walk where all edges are distinct, though nodes may repeat. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node ID (int) or label (str). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Target node ID (int) or label (str). [max_trails]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1000]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of trails to return. Default is `1000`. If `None`, returns all trails (dangerous for large graphs). If limit exceeded, returns partial list. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of trails, where each trail is a sequence of node IDs. If `max_trails=` exceeded, returns first `max_trails=` trails found. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or target node not found in graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Same enumeration as `count_trails()`, but every trail is materialized as its full node sequence, which changes the memory picture entirely: even a modest $1{,}000$ trails at $50$ nodes apiece is several megabytes of Python lists, and the counts explode faster than the graph size does, so `max_trails=` must almost always be set to something sane. Because edges are unique but nodes are not, a returned trail can revisit nodes freely, which is exactly what makes trails useful for reasoning about redundant routing, network vulnerability, or edge-covering tours where the walker may pass through a hub several times. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Unlike `count_trails()`, this returns the actual node sequences, so on a triangle we get back both routes from `A` to `C` explicitly: ::: {#e5d67688 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") ) trails = graph.enumerate_trails("A", "C") # Returns [['A', 'C'], ['A', 'B', 'C']] trails ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'C'], ['A', 'B', 'C']] ``` ::: ::: Node IDs work the same way as labels: ::: {#a82cebee .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_node(label="start") graph.add_node(label="end") graph.add_edge("start", "end") start_id = graph.get_id_from_label("start") end_id = graph.get_id_from_label("end") # Returns 1 (the single direct trail) len(graph.enumerate_trails(start_id, end_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: `max_trails` bounds how many trails are collected, which matters once a graph is large enough that enumerating every trail would be expensive: ::: {#6d7e43e7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} G = ec.karate_club() node_ids = list(G.get_node_ids(limit=None)) source_id = node_ids[0] target_id = node_ids[-1] trails = G.enumerate_trails(source=source_id, target=target_id, max_trails=100) # At most 100 trails are returned, even if more exist len(trails) <= 100 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: With the returned trails in hand, it's easy to summarize how their lengths vary: ::: {#c385dce3 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} lengths = [len(trail) - 1 for trail in trails] # -1 to count edges, not nodes # Returns (shortest, longest) trail length found (min(lengths), max(lengths)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (4, 67) ``` ::: :::
